AI is a branch of computer science focused on

language

them to predict or decide.

1950 — The Beginning
ALAN TURING
“Can a machine think?”
This was exactly Alan Turing’s question. He 
proposed what is now known as the Turing Test 
— a way to judge whether a machine can 
exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable 
from a human.
Imagine chatting online. One participant is a human, 
the other a computer. If the judge can’t tell which is 
which — the computer passes the test.

A Simple Definition
Machine Learning is the process of enabling computers to learn patterns from 
data and use those patterns to make predictions or decisions — without being 
explicitly programmed for every situation.
Real-Life Example: Netflix
Does Netflix know your favorite movie? No. It studies what you watch, what 
you skip, and how you rate things — then it predicts what you might like next. 
That's Machine Learning in action.

cannot learn without it.
Common sources:

Clean Data

Step 3–4: Feature Engineering & Split Data
Feature Engineering
Features are the input variables a model learns 
from. Better features often help more than a 
fancier algorithm.
Example:
• Date of purchase → Day of week, Month, 
Weekend/weekday
• Birth Year = 2004 → Age = 22 (often more 
useful)
Split Data
Never train and test on the same data — usually 
an 80 / 20 split.

Step 5–6: Train & Evaluate the Model
Train the Model
The algorithm studies the training data and 
learns patterns — no one explicitly programs 
every rule.
Example — spam detection. The model learns 
from:
• Certain words
• Email length
• Links
• Sender information
Evaluate the Model
“How do we know if the model is good?” We test 
it on unseen data.
Common evaluation metrics:
• Accuracy
• Precision & Recall
• F1-score
• Mean Squared Error (regression)

37 Copyright @ 2026 NTI 
Step 7–8: Deploy & Predict
Deploy the Model
A trained model is useful only once people can 
actually use it — by integrating it into a real 
application:
• Website / mobile app
• Hospital system
• Banking software
Predict
The model receives new data and produces 
predictions:
New customer → Model→
“Likely to buy” or “Not likely to buy”
Summary: the pipeline isn't just about training a model — most of the work is preparing the data and 
making the model usable.

Challenges of AI (1/2)
Bias
If training data is biased, the model learns 
and repeats those unfair patterns
Privacy
AI often relies on personal data — medical 
records, location, face and voice — raising 
concerns about collection and storage.
Security
Systems can be attacked: adversarial 
examples that fool classifiers, data 
poisoning, and model theft.
Fake Images & Video
Generative AI can create convincing 
deepfakes, spreading misinformation and 
blurring real vs. fake.

40 Copyright @ 2026 NTI 
Challenges of AI (2/2)
Hallucinations
LLMs sometimes generate incorrect or 
fabricated information while sounding 
confident. Always verify AI output for 
important decisions.
Ethics
Should AI make medical decisions? Who is 
responsible if an autonomous car causes 
an accident? How do we ensure fairness 
and transparency?
Job Automation
AI automates repetitive tasks while 
creating new roles requiring AI skills — it is 
more likely to change jobs than replace all 
workers.
Explainability
Models can be accurate yet hard to 
explain — critical in fields like healthcare 
and finance where decisions affect 
people's lives.

What does "it" refer to? A good model must understand context.
The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired.
✓ it → animal (tired animal, not the street)

PART 2
What is Attention?
Imagine reading a book. When answering a question, you don't re-read every page equally.
You focus only on the relevant parts. Humans use attention — and neural networks can too.
Sentence:
Ahmed likes eating green apples.
Question: "Who likes apples?"

PART 3
Attention Intuition
Sentence
The cat sat on the red chair.
Task: Predict next word after "chair"
Not every word matters equally!
Attention learns WHERE to look,
not everywhere equally.
Attention Weights
The 0.02
cat 0.10
sat 0.08
red 0.30
chair 0.50
Key Idea: Attention learns WHERE to look — not everywhere equally.

PART 4
Query, Key & Value
Think of Google Search: you type a Query → Google compares it against Keywords (Keys) of billions of pages → 
Returns the most relevant content (Values).
Q
Query
What am I looking for?
K
Key
What information do I contain?
V
Value
The actual information.
How each word generates Q, K, V:
Word Embedding
Linear (Q)
Linear (K)
Linear (V)

PARTS 5&6
Scaled Dot-Product Attention
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QKᵀ / √dₖ ) · V
1 Similarity (QKᵀ)
Compute dot product of Query with every Key.
Higher score = more relevant.
2 Scaling (÷ √dₖ)
Large vectors produce huge values → unstable softmax.
Dividing by √dₖ keeps gradients stable.
3 Softmax
Converts raw scores [4, 2, 1]
into probabilities [0.84, 0.11, 0.05] that sum to 1.
4 Weighted Sum (· V)
Final output = 0.84·V₁ + 0.11·V₂ + 0.05·V₃
Blends values by importance.
Example: Q=[1,2] · K₁=[2,2] = 6 vs Q=[1,2] · K₂=[-1,3] = 5 → K₁ wins more attention

PART 7
Numerical Example: "I love AI"
Step 1 — Assign Embeddings
I → [1, 0]
love → [0, 1]
AI → [1, 1]
Step 2 — Compute Q·K Scores (for word "I")
Q·K(I) = [1,0]·[1,0] = 1
Q·K(love) = [1,0]·[0,1] = 0
Q·K(AI) = [1,0]·[1,1] = 1
Step 3 — Apply Softmax (÷ √2 ≈ 1.41)
Scaled: [0.71, 0, 0.71]
Softmax → [0.42, 0.16, 0.42]
Step 4 — Weighted Sum of Values
Output = 0.42·[1,0] + 0.16·[0,1] + 
0.42·[1,1]
= [0.84, 0.58]

PART 8
Self-Attention
The boy kicked the ball because he was angry.
What does "he" refer to? → Self-attention lets each word attend to every other word.
The boy kicked the ball because he was angry
attends to
Every word communicates with every other word.
In self-attention, Q, K, and V all come from the SAME sequence.
Each word asks: "Which other words are most relevant to understanding me?"

10
Attention scores for every word, against every other word — laid out as a grid.
SENTENCE
I
love
AI
Each token will both ask a question 
(row) and be asked about (column).

I 0.6 0.2 0.2
love 0.2 0.5 0.3
AI 0.1 0.3 0.6
Columns — who is being 
attended to?
Rows
— who is
asking?

11
Why only one attention? Different heads learn different relationships.
Head 1
Grammar

Verb–object
Head 3
Pronouns

PART 11
Positional Encoding
12
Attention ignores order — it only looks at content, not position.
WITHOUT POSITIONAL INFORMATION
Dog bites man = Man bites dog
As a bag of words, both sentences contain the exact same tokens — attention alone can't tell them apart.
We need to inject positional information — a signal for where each word sits in the sequence.
sin Sine waves
Each position gets a unique wave pattern 
across the embedding dimensions — a 
fingerprint for position.
cos Cosine waves
Paired with sine at different frequencies, so 
every position maps to a distinct, smooth 
code.
These positional codes are added to word embeddings, so the model knows both what a word is and where it 
sits.

PART 12
Masked Attention
13
Needed for GPT. A model predicting the next word can't be allowed to peek at it.
SENTENCE
I love AI
WHILE PREDICTING
love
CANNOT PEEK AT
AI
Future words are masked — set to −∞ before softmax, so they receive zero attention weight.
I love AI
I ✓ ✕ ✕
love ✓ ✓ ✕
AI ✓ ✓ ✓
Masking enforces left-to-right causality — each word can only attend to itself and what came before it.

PART 13
Encoder vs. Decoder Attention
14
Three flavors of attention, depending on where they sit in the architecture.
ENCODER
Self-Attention
Everyone talks to everyone — full, 
unmasked attention across the whole 
input.
DECODER
Masked Self-Attention
Cannot see future tokens — each 
position only attends to itself and the 
past.
ENCODER → DECODER
Cross-Attention
Decoder queries attend to the 
encoder's output representations.
ENCODER
Input tokens
Self-Attention (full)
DECODER
Output tokens (so far)
Masked Self-AttentionCross-
Attention
Same attention mechanism, three jobs: full context (encoder), causal generation (decoder), and bridging the 
two (cross-attention).

PART 14
The Cost of Attention
15
Every word compares itself to every other word — that comparison is what makes attention powerful, and expensive.
n words n² comparisons
Every query attends to every key — so cost grows quadratically with sequence length.
EXAMPLE
1,000
tokens
1,000,000
pairwise comparisons
Efficient variants — Linear Attention and FlashAttention reduce this cost — through approximation or smarter memory 
access — to make long-context models practical.
Quadratic cost is the central scaling bottleneck of the Transformer — and a major area of ongoing research.

PART 15
Attention in Large Language Models
16
The same building blocks from Parts 9–13, deployed inside the models you actually use.
GPT
Masked Self-Attention
Generates text one token at a time, attending only to itself and what came 
before — same causal mask from Part 12.
BERT
Bidirectional Self-Attention
Reads the whole sentence at once, with every token attending to every other 
token — built for understanding, not generation.
Encoder–Decoder
Self-Attention + Cross-Attention
Translation-style models use encoder self-attention, decoder masked self-
attention, and cross-attention to connect them — the full architecture from 
Part 13.
Attention isn't one technique — it's a flexible mechanism reused across very different model families and 
goals.

PART 16
Limitations of Attention
17
Attention is powerful, but not free — practical constraints to keep in mind.
Quadratic memory and computation
Cost scales as O(n²) with sequence length — the bottleneck 
explored in Part 14.
Degraded performance on long 
sequences
Even when compute allows it, quality can drop as context 
grows very long.
Attention weights aren't reliable 
explanations
High attention to a token doesn't always mean it drove the 
model's reasoning.
Motivates efficient attention research
Linear Attention, FlashAttention, and similar methods exist 
to address these limits.
Understanding these limits is what's driving the next generation of long-context, efficient Transformer 
designs.

DENSITY-BASED CLUSTERING
DBSCAN
Discovering Clusters of Arbitrary Shape & Detecting Outliers
Prepared by Nancy Ahmed

What is DBSCAN?
Density-Based Spatial Clustering
of Applications with Noise
An unsupervised learning algorithm used for clustering 
data.
Used for:
• Grouping similar points
• Detecting anomalies / outliers
• Discovering clusters of any shape
Why Not K-Means?
K-Means forces spherical clusters using centroids — and fails on 
irregular shapes like rings or curves.
Two ring-shaped clusters — DBSCAN identifies both correctly
2

The Core Idea
Areas with many nearby points form a CLUSTER.
Sparse areas are considered NOISE.
Centroid-Based
(K-Means)
Clusters defined by distance to a central 
point
Density-Based
(DBSCAN)
Clusters defined by how packed points 
are together
Outcome
DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape and 
flags isolated noise points
3

Key Hyperparameters
DBSCAN relies on just two hyperparameters
ε (Epsilon)
The radius around a point that defines its “neighborhood.” 
Answers: “How far should I look for neighbors?”
P ε
MinPts
The minimum number of points required inside a point's ε-
neighborhood for it to be considered “dense.”
Example: MinPts = 5 → a point needs at least 5 
neighbors nearby to be considered dense.
Together, ε and MinPts define what “dense” means for the 
dataset.
4

Types of Points
The most important concept in DBSCAN — ε = 2, MinPts = 4
Core Point
Has at least MinPts neighbors within ε. 
Forms the dense interior of a cluster.
Border Point
Doesn't have enough neighbors itself, 
but lies within ε of a Core Point.
Noise Point
Neither core nor border — an isolated 
point that belongs to no cluster.
5

How DBSCAN Works
1
Choose ε and MinPts
2
Pick an unvisited point
3
Count its neighbors 
within ε
4
If neighbors ≥ MinPts, 
start a new cluster
5
Expand the cluster via 
neighboring core 
points
6
Repeat until every 
point is processed
Density Reachability
Point B is density-reachable from A if A is a core point 
and B lies within A's ε-neighborhood.
A B
Density Connectivity
Two points belong to the same cluster if they're 
connected through a chain of core points.
6

Example Walkthrough
ε = 2 MinPts = 4
Dataset
Dense area → Cluster
Single point → Noise (not enough neighbors)
Result
Top group: 
Dense area → forms one cluster
Single point: 
Not enough neighbors → classified as noise
7

Choosing ε and MinPts
Choosing ε
Too Small
Many small clusters & many noise points — under-clustering
Too Large
Everything merges into one cluster — over-clustering
Choosing MinPts
2D data: MinPts = 4
Higher dimensions: MinPts ≥ features + 1 (often 5, 10, or 20)
K-Distance Graph
Best method to pick ε: compute distance to the k-th nearest neighbor 
for each point, sort, plot, and look for the ‘elbow’ — that value is a 
good ε.
8

Advantages & Disadvantages
Advantages
1 No need to specify K
Automatically discovers the number of clusters, unlike K-Means.
2 Detects outliers
Noise points are naturally identified as part of the algorithm.
3 Handles arbitrary shapes
Finds circular, curved, and irregular clusters.
4 Robust to noise
Performs well even with noisy datasets.
Disadvantages
1 Sensitive to ε
A poorly chosen ε gives bad results — too small or too large changes 
everything.
2 Struggles with varying densities
A single ε may not work for clusters of different densities.
9

DBSCAN vs K-Means
Feature K-Means DBSCAN
Requires K Yes No
Detects Noise No Yes
Arbitrary Shapes No Yes
Centroid Based Yes No
Density Based No Yes
DBSCAN's defining strength is that it adapts to the data's 
density — rather than forcing data into a predefined number of 
spherical groups.

Decision Tree Algorithm Pseudocode
1. Place the best attribute of the dataset at the root of the tree.
2. Split the training set into subsets. Subsets should be made in such a way that 
each subset contains data with the same value for an attribute.
3. Repeat step 1 and step 2 on each subset until you findleaf nodes in all the 
branches of the tree.

source: decision tree & ensemble learning & random forest.pdf
text:
Decision Tree Algorithm Pseudocode
• Assign all training instances to the root of the tree. Set curent node to root node.
• For each attribute
• Partition all data instances at the node by the value of the attribute.
• Compute the information gain ratio from the partitioning.
• Identify feature that results in the greatest information gain ratio. Set this feature 
to be the splitting criterion at the current node.
• If the best information gain ratio is 0, tag the current node as a leaf and return.
• Partition all instances according to attribute value of the best feature.
• Denote each partition as a child node of the current node.
• For each child node:
• If the child node is “pure” (has instances from only one class) tag it as a leaf and return.
• If not set the child node as the current node and recurse to step 2

Entropy
• Entropy is a scientific concept as well as a measurable physical 
property that is most commonly associated with a state of disorder, 
randomness, or uncertainty.
• In information theory, the entropy of a random variable is the average 
level of “surprise”, or “uncertainty” inherent to the variable’s possible 
outcomes.
• In the context of Decision Trees, entropy is a measure of disorder or 
impurity in a node. 
• Thus, a node with more variable composition, such as 2Pass and 2 Fail 
would be considered to have higher Entropy than a node which has 
only pass or only fail.

AdaBoost
• AdaBoost is a boosting algorithm, which also works on the principle of the
stagewise addition method where multiple weak learners are used for getting
strong learners.

What Makes AdaBoost Different
• AdaBoost is similar to Random Forests in the sense that the predictions are taken from
many decision trees. However, there are three main differences that make AdaBoost
unique:
• First, AdaBoost creates a forest of stumps rather than trees. A stump is a tree that is made of only
one node and two leaves.
• Second, the stumps that are created are not equally weighted in the final decision. Stumps that
create more error will have less say in the final decision.
• Lastly, the order in which the stumps are made is important, because each stump aims to reduce
the errors that the previous stump(s) made.

How AdaBoost Works
• Step 1: A weak classifier (e.g. a decision stump) is made on top of the training data based on the weighted samples. Here, 
the weights of each sample indicate how important it is to be correctly classified. Initially, for the first stump, we give all 
the samples equal weights.
• Step 2: We create a decision stump for each variable and see how well each stump classifies samples to their target 
classes. 
• Step 3: More weight is assigned to the incorrectly classified samples so that they're classified correctly in the next decision 
stump. Weight is also assigned to each classifier based on the accuracy of the classifier, which means high accuracy = high 
weight!
• Step 4: Reiterate from Step 2 until all the data points have been correctly classified, the error function does not change, or 
the maximum iteration level has been reached.

• it is easier to use with less need for tweaking parameters.
• Theoretically, AdaBoost is not prone to overfitting though there is no concrete
proof for this.
• AdaBoost can be used to improve the accuracy of your weak classifiers hence
making it flexible.
• It has now being extended beyond binary classification and has found use cases

Disadvantages of AdaBoost
• Boosting technique learns progressively, it is important to ensure that you have
quality data.

Gradient Boosting components
• Loss Function - The role of the loss function is to estimate how good the model is at making predictions with 
the given data. For example, if we're trying to predict the weight of a person depending on some input 
variables (a regression problem), then the loss function would be something that helps us find the difference
between the predicted weights and the observed weights. 
• Weak Learner - A weak learner is one that classifies our data but does so poorly, perhaps no better than 
random guessing. 
• Additive Model - This is the iterative and sequential approach of adding the trees (weak learners) one step 
at a time. After each iteration, we need to be closer to our final model. In other words, each iteration should 
reduce the value of our loss function.

Gradient Boosting
• Gradient Boosting is the boosting algorithm that works on the principle of the stagewise addition 
method, where multiple weak learning algorithms are trained and a strong learner algorithm is 
used as a final model from the addition of multiple weak learning algorithms trained on the same

simply return the mean of the particular column, and the residual for output of the first weak 
learner algorithm will be calculated which will be used as output or target column for next weak 
learning algorithm which is to be trained.
• Following the same pattern, the second weak learner will be trained and the residuals will be 
calculated which will be used as an output column again for the next weak learner, this is how this 
process will continue until we reach zero residuals.
• In gradient boosting the dataset should be in the form of numerical or categorical data and the 
loss function using which the residuals are calculated should be differential at all points.

AdaBoost Vs. Gradient Boosting
• Both AdaBoost and Gradient Boost learn sequentially from a weak set of learners.
• A strong learner is obtained from the additive model of these weak learners. The main focus here is to learn from the shortcomings at each step in the iteration.
• AdaBoost requires users specify a set of weak learners (alternatively, it will randomly generate a set of weak learner before the real learning process).
• It increases the weights of the wrongly predicted instances and decreases the ones of the correctly predicted instances. The weak learner thus focuses more on the
difficult instances. After being trained, the weak learner is added to the strong one according to its performance (so-called alpha weight). The higher it performs,
the more it contributes to the strong learner.
• On the other hand, gradient boosting doesn’t modify the sample distribution. Instead of training on a newly sampled distribution, the weak learner trains on the
remaining errors of the strong learner.
• It is another way to give more importance to the difficult instances. At each iteration, the pseudo-residuals are computed and a weak learner is fitted to these
pseudo-residuals.
• Then, the contribution of the weak learner to the strong one isn’t computed according to its performance on the newly distributed sample but using a gradient
descent optimization process. The computed contribution is the one minimizing the overall error of the strong learner.

• Frequently has remarkable predicting accuracy.
• Numerous choices for hyperparameter adjustment and the ability to optimize various loss

Disadvantages of Gradient Boosting

XGBoost
• XGBoost improves upon the base GBM framework through systems 
optimization and algorithmic enhancements.

System Optimization:
• Parallelization: XGBoost approaches the process of sequential tree building using parallelized implementation. This is possible due to the
interchangeable nature of loops used for building base learners; the outer loop that enumerates the leaf nodes of a tree, and the second inner loop
that calculates the features. This nesting of loops limits parallelization because without completing the inner loop (more computationally demanding
of the two), the outer loop cannot be started. Therefore, to improve run time, the order of loops is interchanged using initialization through a global
scan of all instances and sorting using parallel threads. This switch improves algorithmic performance by offsetting any parallelization overheads in
computation.
• Tree Pruning: The stopping criterion for tree splitting within GBM framework is greedy in nature and depends on the negative loss criterion at the
point of split. XGBoost uses ‘max_depth’ parameter as specified instead of criterion first, and starts pruning trees backward. This ‘depth-first’
approach improves computational performance significantly.
• Hardware Optimization: This algorithm has been designed to make efficient use of hardware resources. This is accomplished by cache awareness by
allocating internal buffers in each thread to store gradient statistics. Further enhancements such as ‘out-of-core’ computing optimize available disk
space while handling big data-frames that do not fit into memory.

Algorithmic Enhancements:
• Regularization: It penalizes more complex models through both LASSO (L1) and Ridge (L2) regularization to
prevent overfitting.
• Sparsity Awareness: XGBoost naturally admits sparse features for inputs by automatically ‘learning’ best
missing value depending on training loss and handles different types of sparsity patterns in the data more
efficiently.
• Weighted Quantile Sketch: XGBoost employs the distributed weighted Quantile Sketch algorithm to
effectively find the optimal split points among weighted datasets.
• Cross-validation: The algorithm comes with built-in cross-validation method at each iteration, taking away
the need to explicitly program this search and to specify the exact number of boosting iterations required in
a single run.

XGBoost
• XGBoost is also a boosting machine learning algorithm, which is the next version on top of the gradient boosting algorithm.
• The full name of the XGBoost algorithm is the eXtreme Gradient Boosting algorithm, as the name suggests it is an extreme
version of the previous gradient boosting algorithm.
• The main difference between GradientBoosting is XGBoost is that XGboost uses a regularization technique in it. In simple
words, it is a regularized form of the existing gradient-boosting algorithm.
• Due to this, XGBoost performs better than a normal gradient boosting algorithm and that is why it is much faster than that
also.
• XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting) is a specific implementation of GBM that introduces additional enhancements. XGBoost
performs better than a normal gradient boosting algorithm and is much faster. A primary advantage of XGBoost over GBM are
the greater set of hyper parameters that are able to be tuned.
• XGBoost provides a parallel tree boosting (also known as GBDT, GBM) that solve many data science problems in a fast and
accurate way.

Common Schedulers
1 Step Decay
Reduce LR after a fixed number of epochs.

2 Exponential Decay
Gradually decrease LR every step, following an exponential curve.

Reduce LR only when validation performance stops improving.

PA R T 2 · 4 . Weight Initialization 10
A Simple Initialization Rule of Thumb
Xavier / Glorot Initialization
Used with: Sigmoid · Tanh
Maintains reasonable variance of activations as information 
passes through layers.

Used with: ReLU

PA R T 2 · 5 . Batch Normalization 11
Keeping Activations Well-Scaled
Before Normalization
Some activations very large, some very small → training 
becomes difficult.
After Batch Normalization
Activations are normalized using mini-batch statistics — stable, 
comparable scale across the network.
x̂ = (x − μ_B) / √(σ²_B + ε) y = γ · x̂ + β
μ_B = batch mean · σ²_B = batch variance · γ, β = learnable scale & shift
Why use it?
✓ Stabilizes training
✓ Allows larger learning rates in some cases
✓ Can provide a mild regularization effect
Caution
BatchNorm helps a great deal, but it does not 
completely solve vanishing or exploding gradients.

PA R T 2 · 8 . Regularization 14
How Can We Reduce Overfitting?
Regularization discourages the model from relying on overly complex parameter configurations.
L2 Regularization
L_total = L_data + λ Σ wᵢ²
Penalizes squared weights. Encourages smaller weights 
overall. Closely related to weight decay.
Rarely produces exact zeros
L1 Regularization
L_total = L_data + λ Σ |wᵢ|
Penalizes absolute weight values. Pushes some weights to 
exactly zero, producing a sparse model.
Useful for feature selection
Large weights → large penalty → the optimizer is nudged toward smaller, simpler weight configurations — reducing the 
model's tendency to overfit.

PA R T 2 · 9 . Dropout 15
Randomly Disabling Neurons During Training
Before Dropout — all neurons active
Every neuron participates every step.
One training step — Dropout ON
✕ ✕
✕
A random subset is disabled each step — the network can't lean on 
any single neuron.
Training
Dropout: ON
Forces the network to build robust, distributed representations 
instead of depending on specific neurons.
Inference
Dropout: OFF
All neurons are used for predictions. Frameworks like PyTorch switch 
this automatically between train/eval modes.

The Motivation Behind Feature Selection
Curse of Dimensionality

Key Insight: More features ≠ Better performance. The goal is to find the minimal set of features that maximizes predictive

What is Feature S election?
Definition:The process of selecting a subset of relevant features for use in model construction, removing redundant 
or irrelevant variables.
Feature S election
● Selects a subset of original features
● Preserves interpretability
● Feature names remain meaningful
Example:
From {age, income, height, zip} → select {age, income}
VS
Feature Extraction
● Creates new featuresfrom originals
● Transforms the representation
● May lose direct interpretability
Example:
PCA, LDA — create synthetic components

Why Feature S election Matters
Accuracy
Removing noisy or irrelevant features improves predictive

patterns in the data.
Interpretability
Fewer features make models easier to understand, explain, 
and debug — critical for domains like healthcare and 
finance.
Computation Cost
Reduces training time and memory requirements 
significantly — especially important for large-scale 
applications.
Overfitting Prevention
Prevents models from memorizing noise in high-
dimensional data, leading to better performance on unseen 
data.

SECTION 1 · FILTER METHODS
Filter Methods Overview
• Rank features using statistical tests, independent of any ML model
• “Model-independent” — score is computed before any model is trained
• Fast, scalable pre-processing step, especially for high-dimensional data
• Common tests: correlation, chi-square, information gain, variance
Typical Workflow
1. Compute a statistical score per feature
▼
2. Rank features by score
▼
3. Keep top-k or above-threshold features
▼
4. Pass selected features to any model
ADVANTAGES
• Very fast, low 
computational cost
• Scales to thousands of 
features
• Works with any 
downstream model
LIMITATIONS
• Ignores feature 
interactions
• No feedback from actual 
model performance
• Threshold / k choice can 
be arbitrary
Comparison Diagram
Dataset ▶ Statistical Test ▶ Selected Features ▶ ML Model

FILTER METHOD
Information Gain
• Entropy: measures impurity / disorder in the target labels
• Information Gain: reduction in entropy after splitting on a feature
• Higher IG → feature separates classes more cleanly
• Works well for classification, especially with categorical or 
discretized features
Entropy
H(S) = −Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ)
Information Gain
IG(S,A) = H(S) − Σ (|Sv|/|S|)·H(Sv)
ADVANTAGES
• Captures non-linear 
relevance
• Intuitive, used inside 
decision trees
LIMITATIONS
• Biased toward high-
cardinality features
• Needs binning for 
continuous data
information_gain.py
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest
# score each feature's mutual info with the target
scores = mutual_info_classif(X_train, y_train)
# keep the 10 features with highest information gain
selector = SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=10)
X_new = selector.fit_transform(X_train, y_train)
selected = X_train.columns[selector.get_support()]
print(selected)
HOW IT WORKS
– mutual_info_classif() scores each feature vs. the target
– SelectKBest(k=10) keeps only the top-10 scoring features
– get_support() returns a boolean mask of the kept columns

FILTER METHODS
Mean Absolute Difference & Dispersion Ratio
Mean Absolute Difference (MAD)
• Average absolute deviation of each value from the feature mean
• Higher MAD → feature varies more → potentially more informative
• Cheap alternative to variance; less sensitive to large outliers
Formula
MAD = (1/n) Σ |xᵢ − x̄|
mean_absolute_difference.py
import numpy as np
def mad(column):
return np.mean(np.abs(column - column.mean()))
# score every numeric column
mad_scores = X_train.apply(mad)
top_features = mad_scores.sort_values(
ascending=False).head(10).index
Dispersion Ratio
• Ratio of arithmetic mean (AM) to geometric mean (GM) of a feature
• Ratio near 1 → values are similar → low information
• Larger ratio → greater spread → feature likely more useful
Formula
DR = AM(x) / GM(x), GM = (Πxᵢ)^(1/n)
dispersion_ratio.py
import numpy as np
def dispersion_ratio(column):
col = column[column > 0] # GM needs > 0
am = col.mean()
gm = np.exp(np.log(col).mean())
return am / gm
dr_scores = X_train.apply(dispersion_ratio)

Wrapper Methods
Model-based iterative approaches
that use predictive performance to guide selection

Wrapper Methods: RFE, Forward & Backward Selection
R
Recurs ive Feature 
Elimination
1 . Start with all features
2. Train model, rank features
3. Remove weakest feature(s)
4. Repeat until target count
Best for: When you know desired feature 
count
F Forward Selection
1 . Start with no features
2. Test adding each feature
3. Add the one that improves performance 
most
4. Repeat until stopping criterion
Best for: When few features are expected
B Backward Elimination
1 . Start with all features
2. Test removing each feature
3. Remove the least significant
4. Repeat until all remaining are significant
Best for: When most features are relevant
Common Workflow Pattern
Select Subset Train Model Evaluate Score Update S ubset Iterate

SECTION 2 · WRAPPER METHODS
Wrapper Methods Overview
• Search for feature subsets by repeatedly training and 
evaluating a model
• Filter = statistics only; Wrapper = actual model performance as 
the score
• Explores feature interactions the model itself would see
• Cost scales with dataset size × number of subsets tried
ADVANTAGES
• Accounts for feature 
interactions
• Optimized directly for chosen 
model
LIMITATIONS
• Computationally expensive
• Risk of overfitting to validation 
set
Wrapper Search Loop
Dataset
▼
Train Model on Feature Subset
▼
Evaluate Subset Performance
▼
Keep or Reject Features

WRAPPER METHOD
Forward Selection
• Starts with an empty feature set
• Adds the single feature that most improves model performance
• Repeats until no further improvement (or target count reached)
• Good when few features are truly relevant, out of many candidates
Step-by-Step
1. Start with 0 features
▼
2. Test adding each remaining feature
▼
3. Permanently add the best performer
▼
4. Repeat until stop condition is met
forward_selection.py
from sklearn.feature_selection import (
SequentialFeatureSelector)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
sfs = SequentialFeatureSelector(
model, n_features_to_select=8,
direction='forward', cv=5)
sfs.fit(X_train, y_train)
X_new = sfs.transform(X_train)
HOW IT WORKS
– direction='forward' grows the subset one feature at a time
– cv=5 scores each candidate with 5-fold cross-validation
– n_features_to_select fixes how many features to end with

WRAPPER METHOD
Backward Elimination
• Starts with ALL features included
• Repeatedly removes the least useful feature (by score or p-value)
• Stops when removing further hurts performance
• Computationally heavier than forward selection on large feature sets
ADVANTAGES
• Considers full context of all features
• Often finds strong subsets
LIMITATIONS
• Expensive: many models trained early 
on
• Slow when the initial feature count is 
large
backward_elimination.py
from sklearn.feature_selection import (
SequentialFeatureSelector)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
sbe = SequentialFeatureSelector(
model, n_features_to_select=8,
direction='backward', cv=5)
sbe.fit(X_train, y_train)
HOW IT WORKS
– direction='backward' starts full and removes one feature per round
– Each round drops whichever feature costs the model least
– statsmodels alternative: drop the feature with the highest p-value
– above 0.05 and refit, repeating until all p-values are significant
10

WRAPPER METHOD
Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE)
• Trains the model, ranks features by importance / coefficient weight
• Removes the weakest feature(s), then retrains — recursively
• Continues until the target number of features remains
• Produces a full importance ranking, not just a kept/dropped label
Recursive Elimination
Round 1 Round 2 Round 3 Round 4
rfe.py
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFE
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
rfe = RFE(estimator=model, n_features_to_select=6,
step=1)
rfe.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(rfe.support_) # kept features (bool mask)
print(rfe.ranking_) # 1 = most important
HOW IT WORKS
– estimator provides feature importances / coefficients each round
– step=1 removes one feature per iteration (higher = faster, 
coarser)
– support_ is the final kept mask; ranking_ orders every feature

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

Best Practices for Feature Selection
1 Avoid Data Leakage
Never use information from the test set during feature 
selection. Always fit selectors on training data only. Leakage 
leads to optimistically biased performance estimates.
2 Use Cross-Validation
Validate feature selection within each CV fold to ensure 
selected features generalize across different data splits. This 
prevents overfitting to a particular train/test split.
3 Leverage Domain Knowledge
Combine statistical methods with subject matter expertise. A 
weak statistical feature may be clinically or financially 
important. Domain knowledge improves interpretation.
4 Combine Methods
Use filter methods for initial screening to quickly eliminate 
obviously irrelevant features, then apply wrapper or 
embedded methods for final refinement.

What is Feature Scaling?
Transforming numerical features into a similar range or distribution so that no 
single feature dominates the model.
The Problem Without Scaling:
Feature Range Impact
Age 18 – 60 Small — low influence
Salary 10,000 – 500,000 Huge — DOMINATES the model!
Salary dominates Euclidean distance — the model ignores Age completely!

Algorithms That REQUIRE Scaling
Distance-Based
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
K-Means Clustering
Support Vector Machine (SVM)
Distance calculations are distorted by large-
scale features
Gradient-Based
Logistic Regression
Linear Regression
Neural Networks
PCA
Uneven gradients slow convergence & hurt 
optimization

Algorithms That DON'T Need Scaling
Tree-Based
Models
Decision Trees
Random Forest
XGBoost
LightGBM
Gradient Boosting
Why Trees Don't Need Scaling
Threshold-Based Splits
Trees split data using threshold values (e.g., Age > 30), not 
distances. Scale doesn't affect which split is best.
Feature Independence
Each feature is evaluated independently when finding the best split 
point — no comparison between feature magnitudes.
Order-Preserving
Only the relative order of values matters for tree splits, not their 
absolute magnitude or scale.
⭐ Common Interview Question — Know This!

Normalization — Min-Max Scaling
Formula
x_scaled = ( x − x_min ) ÷ ( x_max − x_min )
Original Scaled [0, 1]
10 (min) 0.0
20 0.5
30 (max) 1.0
Python
from sklearn.preprocessing import 
MinMaxScaler
scaler = MinMaxScaler()
# Fit and transform training data
X_train_scaled = 
scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
# Only transform test data
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)
Advantages
• Keeps values in [0, 1] — bounded range
• Ideal for Neural Networks
• Preserves the shape of the distribution
Disadvantage
• Very sensitive to outliers!
• One huge outlier (e.g. 1000) compresses all other 
values into a tiny range

⭐ Standardization — Z-Score Scaling (Most Important!)
Formula
z = ( x − μ ) ÷ σ
μ Mean of the feature
σ Standard deviation
z Standardized value
Mean after scaling = 0
Std Dev after scaling = 1
Python
from sklearn.preprocessing import 
StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
# Fit on train, transform both
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)
# Check results
print(X_train_scaled.mean()) # → 0.0
print(X_train_scaled.std()) # → 1.0
✅ Advantages
• Works well for most ML models
• Handles normally distributed data well
• Most commonly used scaler in practice
Still moderately affected by extreme outliers

Robust Scaling — Outlier-Resistant
Use this scaler when your dataset has many outliers — it uses median & IQR instead of mean & std.
Formula
x_scaled = ( x − Median ) ÷ IQR
IQR = Q3 − Q1 (Interquartile Range)
Python
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler
scaler = RobustScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)
Outlier Example:
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1000] ← 1000 is a massive outlier
MinMaxScaler All normal values compressed to ~0.0–0.004 ❌ BAD
RobustScaler Normal values spread well, outlier just shifted ✅ GOOD

⚠️ DATA LEAKAGE — The #1 Critical Mistake!
❌ WRONG WAY
# Dangerous! Never do this:
scaler = StandardScaler()
# Fitting on ALL data before split
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
X_train, X_test = train_test_split(
X_scaled
)
# Test data info leaked into scaler!
Test statistics leak into training — model appears better 
than it is!

Interview Questions — Know These!
1 Why do we scale features?
To prevent large-scale features from dominating 
distance/gradient calculations, ensuring fair contribution 
from all features.
2 Which algorithms need scaling?
Distance-based (KNN, SVM, K-Means) and gradient-based 
(Linear/Logistic Regression, Neural Networks, PCA).
3 Why don't tree-based models need scaling?
Trees split on thresholds — they're order-based, not 
distance-based, so scale doesn't affect split quality.
4 Normalization vs Standardization?
MinMax → [0,1], sensitive to outliers. StandardScaler → 
mean=0, std=1, works for most models.
5 What is data leakage in scaling?
Fitting the scaler on all data before splitting — test statistics 
leak into training, giving falsely optimistic results.
6 Why scale AFTER train-test split?
To simulate real-world deployment where we never see test 
data during training.

Key Takeaways
Scaling doesn't make your model smarter — it makes it learn more efficiently
Always fit the scaler on training data only — never on test data
Tree-based models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost) don't need scaling
Use RobustScaler when your data has outliers
Use sklearn Pipelines in production to avoid leakage and simplify code
Always scale before PCA and Neural Networks for best performance

PARAMETER-EFFICIENT FINE-TUNING
Why Not Update All the Weights?
Suppose you want to fine-tune a 7B parameter model. Do you really need to update all 7 billion parameters? No.
Full fine-tuning updates every parameter — costly in GPU memory and storage. Research shows updating only a small subset can reach similar 
performance. PEFT keeps the original weights frozen and trains only a small number of new parameters.
Full Fine-Tuning PEFT
Parameters updated All weights A few parameters
GPU memory High Low
Checkpoint size Large Small adapters
Training speed Slower Faster

THE MOST IMPORTANT PEFT METHOD
LoRA: The Core Idea
Instead of replacing the original weight matrix W, LoRA learns a small 
update on top of it:
W′ = W + BA

Original pretrained weights — frozen, untouched
A and B
Small trainable matrices — only these get updated

Random Oversampling
How It Works
1 Take existing minority class samples
2 Randomly duplicate them until classes are balanced
3 No new information is added — copies are exact
4 Simple and fast to implement
from imblearn.over_sampling import RandomOverSampler
ros = RandomOverSampler()
X_res, y_res = ros.fit_resample(X, y)
Advantages
• Simple and easy to use
• Preserves all minority information
Disadvantages
• High overfitting risk
• Duplicates exact samples — no diversity
• Model memorizes rather than generalizes

SMOTE — The Heart of Oversampling
Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique
Intuition: Creating Synthetic Points
◄ Synthetic
Point
Instead of copying: generate new points between k-nearest neighbors
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
smote = SMOTE(random_state=42)
X_res, y_res = smote.fit_resample(X, y)
Advantages
• Less overfitting than duplication
• More generalized decision boundary
Disadvantages
• May create noisy synthetic samples
• Can produce unrealistic combinations
• Struggles near class overlap

HUGE Common Mistake
Data Leakage
WRONG Workflow
# Apply SMOTE to all data FIRST
X_res, y_res = smote.fit_resample(X, y)
# Then split — WRONG!

# Split FIRST — test set stays untouched
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
X, y, stratify=y, random_state=42)
# Then apply SMOTE only on train
X_tr, y_tr = smote.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)

Five Computer Vision Tasks
Each task asks a more detailed question about the same image.

Image Classification
Main question: What is in the image?
Image classification assigns one label — or a set of labels — to an entire 
image. The model receives the whole picture and outputs a probability for 
each possible class.
• Single-label: the image belongs to one class (e.g. Image → Cat)
• Multi-label: several classes can be predicted at once (e.g. Dog + Car + Person)
• Limitation: tells us WHAT is present, never WHERE it is
If the cat sat in the corner instead of centered, the prediction — and its confidence —
would stay the same. Classification never looks at position.
INPUT IMAGE
IMAGE
↓ CNN
Cat 95%
Dog 5%
Predicted class: Cat (highest probability)
4

Object Localization
Main question: What is the object, and where is it?
Localization goes one step beyond classification: the model still predicts a 
class, but it also predicts the object’s location, usually as a bounding box.
What is a bounding box?
A rectangle that surrounds the object, described by coordinates:
(x, y, w, h) — position (x, y) plus width and height
or (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) — opposite corners of the box
The bounding box tells us approximately WHERE the object is located.
Cat
(x, y, w, h)
5

Classification vs. Localization
Same image — a different level of detail in the answer.
Classification
"What?"
No location returned
Output: class label only
Usually assumes one main subject
Localization
"What + Where?"
Gives a location
Output: class + bounding box
Usually focuses on one main object
6

Object Detection
What objects are present, where are they, and how confident are we?
Detection extends localization to multiple objects in the same image. For 
each object found, the model returns three things:
1 Class what the object is (e.g. Person)
2 Bounding box where the object is (x, y, w, h)
3 Confidence how sure the model is (e.g. 0.97)
Person 0.97
Car 0.91
Dog 0.84
7

Examples of Object Detection Models
Detection can be thought of as localization performed for every object in the image.
YOLO
You Only Look Once
Fast, single-stage detection built for real-time 
use — autonomous driving, surveillance, 
robotics, traffic monitoring.
SSD
Single Shot MultiBox Detector
Another single-stage approach designed to 
perform detection using multiple feature-
map scales to handle different object 
sizes.
Faster R-CNN
Region Proposal + Classification
A two-stage architecture: it proposes 
candidate regions first, then classifies and 
refines each one.
8

Semantic Segmentation
Main question: What class does each pixel belong to?
Instead of one label per image, semantic segmentation assigns a class to 
every pixel, producing a pixel-level class map rather than a rectangle.
Detection gives a rectangle — much of it can be background.
Segmentation keeps only the pixels that truly belong to the object.
Limitation: semantic segmentation knows the class of each pixel, but not 
which individual object it belongs to. Three separate cars are all labeled simply 
"Car" — not Car 1, Car 2, Car 3.
Sky Building
Road Car (same class)
Computer Vision Tasks | Nancy Ahmed 9

Instance Segmentation
Main question: Which individual object does each pixel belong to?
Instance segmentation combines object-level understanding with pixel-
level segmentation: it finds each individual object and produces a 
separate mask for it — even when several objects share the same class.
A mask marks exactly which pixels belong to one specific object (1 = object, 0 = 
background), following its true shape.
Person 1 → Mask 1
Person 2 → Mask 2
Car 1 → Mask 3
Car 2 → Mask 4
Car 1 Car 2 Car 3
Each car gets its own shade + mask — a separate instance.

What is a Mask?
Which pixels belong to an object and which pixels do not.

1 Slow Prediction

What is NLP?
• Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a field within artificial intelligence (AI) and computational linguistics that
focuses on the interaction between computers and human language.
• NLP enables machines to understand, interpret, generate, and respond to human language in a way that is both
meaningful and useful.

Components of NLP
• Natural Language Understanding (NLU) is a subfield of NLP that focuses on the machine's ability to
comprehend and interpret human language. It involves extracting meaningful information and understanding
the context, intent, and semantics of the text.
• Natural Language Generation (NLG) is a subfield of NLP that focuses on creating coherent and contextually
appropriate text based on input data or prompts. It involves generating human-like language from
structured data or other forms of input.

NLP Challenges
• Ambiguity
• Types:
• Lexical Ambiguity: Words with multiple meanings (e.g., "bank" can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river).
• Syntactic Ambiguity: Sentences that can be parsed in multiple ways (e.g., "The man saw the woman with the telescope"
can imply different relationships between the man, woman, and telescope).
• Semantic Ambiguity: Sentences or phrases that can be interpreted in different ways based on context (e.g., "She is looking
for a bank" could mean she’s searching for a financial institution or the side of a river).
• Challenges:
• Developing algorithms that can disambiguate based on context is complex.
• Requires a deep understanding of both linguistic structure and real-world knowledge.

NLP Challenges
• Context Understanding: refers to the ability to comprehend and interpret information within its
relevant circumstances, environment, and background
• Types:
• Long-Range Dependencies: Capturing relationships between words or phrases that are far
apart in a text (e.g., pronoun resolution).
• Conversational Context: Maintaining context over multiple turns in a conversation or
dialogue.
• Challenges:
• Ensuring models remember and correctly interpret context from earlier parts of a
conversation or document.
• Difficult to handle with traditional models but improving with newer architectures like
Transformers.

NLP Challenges
• Handling Diverse and Noisy Data
• Types:
• Social Media and Web Data: Text from social media can be informal, full of slang, 
abbreviations, and errors.
• Multilingual Data: Dealing with multiple languages, dialects, and language variations.
• Challenges:
• Cleaning and preprocessing diverse data sources to ensure quality.
• Building models that generalize well across different languages and informal text.

• Understanding Implicit Meaning
• Types:
• Sarcasm and Irony: Identifying and correctly interpreting sarcastic or ironic statements.
• Cultural and Social Context: Understanding references or implications specific to certain
cultures or social groups.
• Challenges:
• Designing models that can grasp subtle linguistic features and cultural context.
• Training on diverse datasets that cover a wide range of social and cultural nuances.

representation in data.
• Challenges:
• Developing techniques to work effectively with small datasets or using transfer learning from

Text Cleaning
• Text cleaning is a crucial step in natural language processing (NLP)
pipelines, as it prepares raw text data for further analysis and
modeling.
• The goal is to remove or correct parts of the text that could introduce
noise or errors into the analysis.

Advantages of Lowercasing
• Reduces Dimensionality:
• Explanation: By converting all text to lowercase, variations in capitalization (e.g., "Apple" vs. "apple") are normalized. This 
reduces the number of unique tokens or features, simplifying the model and reducing computational complexity.
• Benefit: Helps in creating a more compact and manageable vocabulary, which can improve model efficiency and training 
speed.
• Improves Consistency:
• Explanation: Lowercasing ensures that words are treated consistently regardless of how they are capitalized in the original 
text.
• Benefit: Enhances the accuracy of text matching and similarity measurements, as variations in capitalization no longer affect 
the analysis.
• Simplifies Text Processing:
• Explanation: Many NLP tasks, like text classification or sentiment analysis, do not require distinguishing between "Apple" 
and "apple."
• Benefit: Simplifies the processing pipeline and reduces the need for handling case-specific variations, which can streamline 
text processing.
• Reduces Sparsity:
• Explanation: Lowercasing helps in reducing the sparsity of feature matrices, where each unique capitalization variant would 
otherwise be treated as a distinct feature.
• Benefit: Helps in improving model performance and generalization by reducing the number of features in the feature space.

Disadvantages of Lowercasing
• Loss of Important Information:
• Explanation: Capitalization often conveys important information, such as proper nouns (e.g., "New York" vs. "new york") and 
sentence beginnings. Lowercasing can strip away this information.
• Drawback: Can lead to loss of context or meaning, especially in cases where capitalization is used to convey specific entities 
or emphasis.
• Inconsistent with Certain Use Cases:
• Explanation: In some applications, such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) or document classification, capitalization may 
carry crucial information that distinguishes entities or categories.
• Drawback: Lowercasing might hinder the ability to recognize named entities or classify documents based on capitalized 
terms.
• May Affect Model Performance:
• Explanation: For tasks where capitalization contributes to the understanding of the text (e.g., distinguishing between 
acronyms and regular words), lowercasing can degrade model performance.
• Drawback: May negatively impact the accuracy of models that rely on case-sensitive features or where capitalization plays a 
role in distinguishing meanings.
• Inconsistent with Some Languages:
• Explanation: Not all languages use capitalization in the same way. Some languages (e.g., Chinese) do not use capital letters, 
so lowercasing is less relevant.
• Drawback: The practice may not be applicable or beneficial in all languages, and decisions about text preprocessing should 
consider language-specific conventions.

When to Use Lowercasing
• Use Lowercasing When:
• The task involves analyzing general text where capitalization does not convey 
essential meaning.
• The focus is on text classification, sentiment analysis, or other tasks where 
consistent token representation is more important than case distinctions.
• Avoid Lowercasing When:
• The task involves named entity recognition, where case distinctions are 
important.
• The text contains important case-specific information, such as acronyms, 
titles, or entities where capitalization carries meaning.

Prepreprocessing
• Preprocessing is a crucial step in preparing text data for natural
language processing (NLP) tasks. It helps to standardize and clean text
to improve the performance of NLP models.

Tokenization
• Definition: The process of splitting text into individual tokens, such as words or phrases.
• Techniques:
• Character-based: The simplest tokenization scheme is to feed each character individually to the model. 
• Word Tokenization: Breaking text into words.
• Sentence Tokenization: Splitting text into sentences.
• Subword Tokenization: Handling words that are not in the vocabulary by splitting into subword units 
(state-of-the-art transformer )

Why do we tokenize?
• Tokens are the building blocks of text in the natural language. 
• Therefore, most of the preprocessing and modeling happens at the token level.
• For example, removing stopwords, stemming, lemmatization and many other 
preprocessing steps happen at token levels 
• Even neural network architectures process individual tokens to make sense of the 
document.

Challenges of Character tokenization
• We can see that character-level tokenization ignores any structure in the text and
treats the whole string as a stream of characters.
• Although this helps deal with misspellings and rare words, the main drawback is
that linguistic structures such as words need to be learned from the data.
• This requires significant compute, memory, and data. For this reason, character
tokenization is rarely used in practice.

Word Tokenization
• Instead of splitting the text into characters, we can split it into words and map
each word to an integer.
• Using words from the outset enables the model to skip the step of learning
words from characters, and thereby reduces the complexity of the training
process.

Challenges of word tokenization
• 1. Handling Punctuation and Special Characters
• Separation vs. Retention: Deciding whether punctuation marks (e.g., commas, periods) should be treated as
separate tokens or included with adjacent words can be complex. For example, "Hello, world!" could be
tokenized as ["Hello", ",", "world", "!"] or ["Hello,", "world!"].
• Special Characters: Special characters (e.g., hashtags, @mentions) in social media or URLs can complicate
tokenization. Deciding how to handle these characters requires careful consideration.
• 2. Dealing with Multi-Word Expressions
• Compound Words: Words like "New York" or "machine learning" are often treated as single entities, but
straightforward tokenization might split them into individual words.
• Named Entities: Identifying and properly tokenizing named entities (e.g., "San Francisco", "United Nations") is
challenging as they often appear as multi-word expressions.
• Languages without clear boundaries.
• Some languages, like Chinese or Japanese, don't have clear spaces between words, making tokenization a 
more complex task. Determining where one word ends and another begins can be a significant challenge in 
such languages.
• Handling Out-of-Vocabulary Words
• Unknown Words: Tokenization can struggle with words not seen during training, such as slang or newly
coined terms. Handling these out-of-vocabulary words effectively is challenging.

Subword Tokenization
• The basic idea behind subword tokenization is to combine the best 
aspects of character and word tokenization.

Subword Tokenization
• On the one hand, we want to split rare words into smaller units to allow the 
model to deal with complex words and misspellings. 
• On the other hand, we want to keep frequent words as unique entities so that 
we can keep the length of our inputs to a manageable size.

NLTK
• NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is an open-source Python library for 
Natural Language Processing. It has easy-to-use interfaces for over 50 
corpora and lexical resources such as WordNet, along with a set of 
text processing libraries for classification, tokenization, stemming, and 
tagging.

spaCy
• SpaCy is an open-source Python library that parses and understands large
volumes of text. With available models catering to specific languages (English,
French, German, etc.), it handles NLP tasks with the most efficient
implementation of common algorithms.
• spaCy tokenizer provides the flexibility to specify special tokens that don’t need
to be segmented, or need to be segmented using special rules for each language,
for example punctuation at the end of a sentence should be split off – whereas
“U.K.” should remain one token.

NLTK vs. spaCy
•Use spaCy when: You need fast, accurate, and production-ready NLP tools with pre-
trained models for tasks like tokenization, POS tagging, and NER. It’s ideal for large-scale
applications and real-time processing.
•Use NLTK when: You are focused on educational purposes, research, or need a wide
variety of NLP tools and datasets for prototyping and experimentation. It’s valuable for
learning and exploring different NLP techniques.

Stemming
• Definition: Reducing words to their base or root
form by removing suffixes (e.g., “running” to
“run”).
• Algorithms: Porter Stemmer, Snowball Stemmer.

Lemmatization
• Definition: Reducing words to their base
form using a dictionary-based approach (e.g.,
“better” to “good”).
• Libraries: WordNet Lemmatizer.

Stemming Vs. Lemmatization
Stemming
• In the process of stemming remove 
the suffix of words to get a base 
word.
• Stemming does not always provide 
meaning or dictionary words as its 
result.
• The speed of the stemming process 
is fast.
Lemmatization
• Lemmatization follows lexical 
knowledge to get the root word for 
original one.
• The resulting words of 
lemmatization are always 
meaningful and dictionary words.
• As compared to stemming the 
process, the speed of 
lemmatization is slow.

Stopword Removal
• Definition: Removing common words (e.g., “the”, “and”) that are 
often less informative.
• Purpose: To reduce noise in text data and improve processing 
efficiency.

Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging
• Definition: Assigning grammatical tags to each word (e.g., noun, verb, 
adjective).
• Techniques: Rule-based taggers, statistical models like Hidden Markov Models 
(HMMs).

Named Entity Recognition (NER)
• Definition: Identifying and classifying entities (e.g., names, dates, locations) 
within text.
• Techniques: Rule-based approaches, machine learning classifiers.

Parsing
• Definition: Analyzing the grammatical structure of sentences.
• Parsing can be more complex than POS tagging because it involves 
understanding the grammatical structure and relationships between 
words in a sentence.

Language Detection
• Definition: Identifying the language of the text, is especially useful 
when dealing with multilingual content.

Coreference Resolution
• Coreference resolution is the task of finding all expressions that refer to the same
entity in a text. It is an important step for a lot of higher level NLP tasks that
involve natural language understanding such as document summarization,
question answering, and information extraction.

Padding & Truncation
• Padding and truncation are key preprocessing steps used to ensure that text sequences are of uniform
length, which is essential for many machine learning models and deep learning frameworks.
• Padding is the process of adding special tokens to the end (or beginning) of sequences to ensure they are all
of the same length. This is particularly useful when working with models that require input sequences of a
fixed size.
• Truncation involves cutting off parts of sequences that exceed a certain length. This is used to ensure that
sequences do not exceed the maximum length allowed by the model or processing pipeline.
• Many models (i.e. RNNs/LSTMs, BERT/Transformers) require input sequences to be of a fixed size. Padding
ensures that all sequences are the same length, while truncation ensures sequences are not too long

4 Semantic Chunking (Adaptive)
Description
Dynamically adjusts chunk boundaries using similarity

Better handles varying

IMP LE MEN TATI O N

# Build chunks where similarity >= threshold

for i in range(1, len(sentences)):
if sims[i-1] < threshold:
chunks.append(' '.join(current))
current = [sentences[i]]
else:
current.append(sentences[i])
if current:
chunks.append(' '.join(current))

Feature Engineering
• Feature engineering in Natural Language Processing (NLP) involves transforming raw text data
into numerical features that machine learning models can comprehend and utilize effectively.
• Natural language is inherently ambiguous, with words often having multiple meanings depending
on the context.
• The goal is to represent text in a format that captures semantic meaning, contextual information,
and relationships between words.

Text Representation: One-Hot Encoding
• Represents words as binary vectors, where each word has a unique index in the vector.
• Converts words into a high-dimensional space, with each dimension corresponding to a unique 
word.

Text Representation: One-Hot Encoding
• Advantages:
• Simple Representation: Each category or word is represented by a
binary vector, making it easy to understand and implement.
• Disadvantages:
• Dimensionality: It can lead to a high-dimensional feature space,
especially when dealing with large categorical variables
• Sparse Representation: It produces sparse matrices with mostly
zeros, which can lead to memory inefficiency and computational
overhead.

Text Representation: Bag of Words (BoW)
• Introduced in the 1950s and 1960s, the Bag of 
Words model is one of the earliest and 
simplest approaches for representing text.
• Represents text as a collection of unique 
words disregarding grammar or word order.
• Creates a matrix where rows represent 
documents and columns represent unique 
words, with values indicating word 
occurrence frequencies.
• Unlike one-hot encoding, BoW captures word 
frequency rather than binary presence.

BOW Advantages 
• Simplicity: BoW is a relatively simple and straightforward approach.
• Efficiency: It's computationally efficient, making it suitable for large datasets.
• Interpretability: The results are often interpretable, as they are based on word
frequencies.

BOW Disadvantages 
• Loss of Semantic Information: BoW treats words as individual units without
considering their order or context. This can lead to the loss of important semantic
information.
• High Dimensionality: BoW representations can become very high-dimensional,
especially for large vocabularies. This can lead to computational challenges and
potential overfitting.
• Sensitivity to Stop Words: Stop words (common words like "the," "and," "a") often
have little semantic value. However, BoW models may assign significant weight to
these words, which can affect the accuracy of the model.
• Inability to Capture Synonymy and Polysemy (words with multiple meanings).

Text Representation: TF-IDF
• Measures the importance of words in a document relative to a corpus.
• Considers both the frequency of a term in a document and its rarity across the
corpus.
• Assigns higher weights to rare terms that are more discriminative.

Text Representation: TF-IDF (Advantage)
• By combining TF and IDF, TF-IDF effectively balances the importance of frequent terms within a document and rare terms
across the corpus, improving the representation of important terms.
• Common words (e.g., "the", "and") that appear frequently across many documents are down-weighted, helping to focus
on more meaningful terms.
• TF-IDF enhances the relevance of documents based on their unique terms. This makes it useful for tasks such as search
engine ranking and document retrieval, where finding documents with unique, relevant terms is crucial.
• The TF-IDF method is relatively straightforward to compute and interpret, making it accessible and effective for various
text processing tasks.
• By emphasizing the importance of unique terms, TF-IDF can improve the accuracy of document similarity measures, such
as cosine similarity.

Text Representation: TF-IDF (Disadvantage)
• TF-IDF represents text as a bag of words, ignoring the order and context of words. This can lead to loss of syntactic and
semantic information.
• The representation can lead to very high-dimensional vectors, especially with large vocabularies. This can result in
increased computational costs and memory usage.
• TF-IDF vectors are often sparse, with many zero values. Sparse representations can be less efficient for certain algorithms
and may require specialized data structures and techniques.
• While TF-IDF can highlight important terms, it may still struggle with extremely rare or domain-specific terms that do not
appear frequently enough across documents to achieve meaningful IDF scores.
• TF-IDF does not address polysemy, where a word may have multiple meanings depending on context. All instances of a
term are treated uniformly, regardless of different meanings.

N-Gram
• N-grams capture local context and word order within a fixed window. This can be useful for understanding
phrases and patterns that are specific to a document or corpus.
• The concept of n-grams is straightforward and easy to implement.
• N-grams are effective for feature extraction in text classification and clustering. They help represent text in a
way that captures specific word combinations that might be relevant for the task.

Neural language models
• Word embedding can help solve the sparsity problem since with can ditch the
one-hot representation of words for their vectors.
• Therefore we can easily build neural language models that can take into
consideration more words than the n-gram models.
• Despite this advantage, however,the number of words considered remains fixed,
and so neural language models still struggle with long-term dependencies.

Unified Semantic Space
• A unified semantic space is a high-dimensional vector space where words, phrases, sentences, or
other linguistic units are represented as vectors.
• These vectors capture the meaning of the linguistic units in a way that allows for meaningful
comparisons and manipulations.

Popular Word Embedding Techniques
• Traditional Word Embedding Techniques
• Advanced Word Embedding Techniques
• Contextualized Word Embedding Techniques

Traditional Word Embedding Techniques
• One-hot encoding:
• One-hot encoding is a simple technique for representing words as binary vectors. Each word 
in the vocabulary is assigned a unique position in the vector, with a value of 1 at that position 
and 0 elsewhere. While this method is straightforward, it suffers from high dimensionality 
and fails to capture any semantic relationships between words.
• TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency):
• TF-IDF is a popular technique for representing text data in a numerical format. It combines 
the frequency of a word in a document (Term Frequency) with the inverse of its frequency 
across all documents (Inverse Document Frequency). This method weighs the importance of 
words, but it does not capture the context or semantic relationships between words.
• Bag of words:
• The bag of words approach represents documents as a vector of word frequencies. Although 
this method can capture the importance of words within a document, it ignores the order of 
words and fails to encode any semantic information.

Neural Word Embedding Techniques
• Word2Vec:
• Word2Vec is a popular neural network-based word embedding technique that captures
semantic relationships between words. It comes in two flavors:
• Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)
• Skip-Gram.
• CBOW predicts the target word based on its context, while Skip-Gram predicts the context
words given the target word. Word2Vec efficiently learns high-quality vector representations,
capturing semantic and syntactic information.
• GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation):
• GloVe constructs a word-word co-occurrence matrix and learns the embeddings by
minimizing the difference between the dot product of word vectors and the logarithm of
their co-occurrence count.
• FastText:
• FastText is an extension of the Word2Vec model, which represents words as the sum of their
subword (n-gram) vectors. This technique allows FastText to capture morphological
information and generate embeddings for out-of-vocabulary words.

Contextualized Word Embedding Techniques
Unlike Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText, which assign a single vector to a word regardless of its context,
contextualized embeddings generate different embeddings for a word depending on its context. These
embeddings are more dynamic and capture meaning based on sentence-level context.
ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models):
Uses a bidirectional LSTM trained on a language modeling task to generate word embeddings. ELMo generates
context-dependent embeddings by considering the entire sentence to determine the representation of each
word.
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers):
A transformer-based model that learns context-aware word embeddings by processing the entire sentence
from both the left and the right. Unlike ELMo, which uses LSTMs, BERT uses self-attention mechanisms and is
bidirectional, capturing richer context.
GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer):
GPT uses a unidirectional transformer to generate context-aware embeddings. It is trained on a large corpus
using a language modeling objective. However, it differs from BERT as it predicts context from left to right.
T5 (Text-to-TextTransfer Transformer):
T5 is another transformer-based model that learns embeddings in a text-to-text framework, where every task
(e.g., classification, translation) is cast into a text generation task. Like BERT, T5 embeddings are context-
sensitive.

Word Embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, 
FastText)
• Word embeddings are a type of text representation that map words or phrases into continuous vector
spaces. 
• These vectors capture semantic meanings and relationships between words, allowing for more nuanced 
text analysis compared to traditional methods like Bag of Words or TF-IDF.
Vector space models capture semantic meaning and relationships between words.
