Word embeddings
• Word embeddings solve these problems by representing each word in the vocabulary by a fairly small (150,
300, 500 dimensional) fixed size vector, called an embedding, which is learned during the training.
• These vectors are created in a manner so that words that appear in similar contexts or have similar
meaning are close together, and they are not sparse vectors like the ones derived from one-hot
embeddings.

How are word embeddings built?
Learning from Data
• Consider the sentence “I love drinking apple smoothies’. If I remove the word ‘apple’ we are left with the following,
incomplete sentence: ‘I love drinking __ smoothies’. If I then gave you this incomplete sentence, and told you to guess the
missing word, you will probably say words like ‘banana’, ‘strawberry’, or ‘apple’, which all have a similar meaning, and usually
appear in similar contexts.
• One of the main ways to learn word embeddings, is by a very similar process to this: the algorithms learn similar word
embedding for words that appear many times in similar contexts by guessing missing words in a huge corpus of text
sentences.
• An embedding matrix E (the matrix that translates a one hot embedding into a word embedding vector) is calculated by
training something similar to a language model (a model that tries to predicts missing words in a sentence) using an Artificial
Neural Network to predict this missing word, in a similar manner to how the weights and biases of the network are calculated.

Word2Vec
• Word2Vec is a word embedding model developed by Google that learns vector representations of words based on
their context in a corpus.
• word2vec is not a singular algorithm, rather, it is a family of model architectures and optimizations that can be
used to learn word embeddings from large datasets.
• Embeddings learned through word2vec have proven to be successful on a variety of downstream natural language
processing tasks.
• Continuous bag-of-words model: predicts the middle word based on surrounding context words. The context
consists of a few words before and after the current (middle) word. This architecture is called a bag-of-words
model as the order of words in the context is not important.
• Continuous skip-gram model: predicts words within a certain range before and after the current word in the same
sentence.

Word2Vec
• Google News Word2Vec:
• Corpus: Trained on 100 billion words from Google News.
• Dimensions: 300-dimensional vectors.
• Vocabulary Size: 3 million words and phrases.
• Download link: Available on Google Code Archive.
• Usage: This is one of the most commonly used pre-trained embeddings in 
many NLP tasks due to its large corpus and robust performance.
• Word2Vec on Wikipedia:
• Corpus: Trained on the Wikipedia corpus.
• Dimensions: Typically 300-dimensional vectors.
• Vocabulary Size: Depends on the version of Wikipedia used for training.
• Usage: Similar to the Google News Word2Vec model but focused on 
Wikipedia articles, making it more domain-specific for encyclopedic 
content.
• Twitter Word2Vec:
• Corpus: Trained on a large collection of tweets.
• Dimensions: Typically 400-dimensional vectors.
• Vocabulary Size: Several million words and phrases.
• Download link: Available through specific research or community-
contributed models.
• Usage: Particularly useful for tasks involving social media text, where the 
vocabulary and language style is different from formal texts.
• Word2Vec from Amazon Reviews:
• Corpus: Trained on Amazon product reviews, focusing on sentiment 
and product-related language.
• Dimensions: Typically 100-300 dimensions.
• Vocabulary Size: Several hundred thousand words.
• Usage: Good for sentiment analysis and product-related NLP tasks 
due to its domain-specific nature.
• Common Crawl Word2Vec:
• Corpus: Trained on Common Crawl data, which is a very large, open 
web corpus.
• Dimensions: Typically 300-dimensional vectors.
• Vocabulary Size: Millions of words and phrases.
• Usage: Useful for tasks where general, web-based text data is 
required.

Word2Vec
• Advantages:
• Captures Semantic Relationships: Learns word vectors that capture meanings and relationships between
words.
• Efficient Training: Uses neural networks for efficient training and representation learning.
• Disadvantages:
• Limited to Fixed Context Window: Context window size is fixed, which may not capture long-range
dependencies.
• No Handling of Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) Words: Cannot generate embeddings for words not seen during
training.

GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation)
• GloVe is an unsupervised learning algorithm for obtaining vector representations for words by
aggregating global word-word co-occurrence statistics from a corpus. Developed by Stanford, it
focuses on word co-occurrence matrices.
• How It Works:
• Co-occurrence Matrix: Constructs a matrix where entries represent how frequently word pairs occur together.
• Factorization: Factorizes the matrix to obtain dense word vectors that capture semantic meaning. The goal is
to approximate the original matrix using these lower-dimensional representations, making it easier to work
with and revealing latent structures.

Common Pre-trained GloVe Embeddings
• GloVe.6B: Trained on a corpus of 6 billion tokens from Wikipedia and Gigaword.
• GloVe.42B: Trained on 42 billion tokens from a larger Common Crawl dataset.
• GloVe.840B: Trained on 840 billion tokens from an even larger Common Crawl dataset.
• GloVe.Twitter: Trained on tweets, capturing informal language and slang.

GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation)
• Advantages:
• Captures Global Statistics: Uses global word co-occurrence information, leading to more accurate
embeddings.
• Disadvantages:
• Fixed Representations: Pre-trained embeddings may not capture domain-specific nuances.
• Requires Large Corpora: Effective when trained on large corpora, which may not be available for all
applications.
• Doesn’t Handle OOV Words: GloVe struggles with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, since the model only
learns embeddings for words that appear in the training corpus.

FastText
• FastText, developed by Facebook's AI Research (FAIR), extends Word2Vec by representing words as bags of character n-
grams. This approach allows FastText to generate embeddings for morphologically rich languages and handle out-of-
vocabulary (OOV) words better.
• How It Works:
• Subword Information: Words are represented as a combination of character n-grams, allowing the model to learn
from subword information.
• Out-of-Vocabulary Words: Can generate embeddings for OOV words by averaging the embeddings of its n-grams.
• Advantages:
• Handles Morphological Variations: Captures subword information, which is useful for morphologically rich
languages.
• OOV Handling: Can generate embeddings for words not seen during training.
• Disadvantages:
• Increased Complexity: Slightly more complex than Word2Vec due to subword representation.
• Potential Overfitting: Can overfit on the n-grams if the corpus is small or noisy.

Choosing the Right Pre-trained Embeddings
• General Tasks: Google News Word2Vec, GloVe.
• Social Media: Twitter Word2Vec.
• Sentiment Analysis: Amazon Reviews Word2Vec.
• Rare Words/Subwords: FastText.

Summary
• Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText are popular methods for learning word embeddings,
each with its unique approach and strengths:
• Word2Vec: Effective for capturing semantic relationships through local context with either CBOW
or Skip-gram. However, it has limitations with out-of-vocabulary words and fixed context windows.
• GloVe: Utilizes global word co-occurrence statistics to create embeddings, capturing broader
semantic relationships. Pre-trained models are available but may not be adaptable to domain-
specific needs.
• FastText: Enhances Word2Vec by incorporating subword information, improving handling of out-
of-vocabulary words and morphological variations.
